meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Without a revolutionary theory there can be no revolutionary movement'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine: Lenin, What Is To Be Done? (1902), Chapter I. The wording with “a” is the 1929 International Publishers translation.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Lenin, What Is To Be Done? (first published March 1902), Chapter I, Section D. This exact English wording, with “a,” comes from the International Publishers translation (copyright 1929). We checked it against a scan of that edition.

source.heading: Where Lenin wrote it

docMeta.dd: What Is To Be Done? Burning Questions of Our Movement
Written autumn 1901 – February 1902; first published March 1902 (Dietz, Stuttgart)
Chapter I, Section D: “Engels on the Importance of the Theoretical Struggle”
International Publishers, New York, Little Lenin Library vol. 4 (copyright 1929)

source.excerpt: This was Marx’s idea, and yet there are people among us who strive—in his name!—to belittle the significance of theory. Without a revolutionary theory there can be no revolutionary movement. This cannot be insisted upon too strongly at a time when the fashionable preaching of opportunism is combined with absorption in the narrowest forms of practical activity.
trail: The sentence opens a paragraph in Chapter I of What Is To Be Done?. In the Moscow Collected Works (vol. 5, 1961) it reads “Without revolutionary theory there can be no revolutionary movement.” Marxists Internet Archive ↗
The popular wording, with “a,” is word for word the International Publishers translation, whose copyright page reads “Copyright, 1929, by International Publishers Co., Inc.” Internet Archive scan ↗
The same wording appears in the London edition from Martin Lawrence, which describes itself as “Reprinted from The Iskra Period, by V. I. Lenin.” Internet Archive ↗

Lenin had used the line before. In The Tasks of the Russian Social-Democrats (written late 1897) he wrote: “It was said long ago that without a revolutionary theory there can be no revolutionary movement.” Marxists Internet Archive ↗
source.excerptNote: Text from the 1929-copyright International Publishers edition. The Moscow Collected Works translation of the same passage reads “Without revolutionary theory…”, with no “a”.

That is before 1931, so in the United States both the original and this translation are in the public domain. Later translations, such as the 1961 Moscow Collected Works version, are separate texts.

author.name: Vladimir Lenin
author.heading: About Vladimir Lenin
author.metaLine: 1870–1924 · Russian revolutionary, Bolshevik leader & Marxist theorist
author.bio: Vladimir Ilyich Lenin (born 22 April 1870, died 21 January 1924) was the Marxist theorist and revolutionary who led the Bolsheviks to power in 1917. He headed the Soviet government until his death. What Is To Be Done? (1902), his case for a disciplined party of professional revolutionaries, is one of his most influential works.

misattribution.heading: Genuine, but with two caveats
misattribution.intro: Lenin really wrote this. Two things are often missed: the exact English wording depends on which translation you use, and Lenin himself presented the idea as an old saying.

items.who: “Without revolutionary theory there can be no revolutionary movement”
items.why: This is the same sentence in the Moscow Collected Works translation (vol. 5, 1961), which leaves out “a.” Both versions are faithful. The version with “a” is the earlier International Publishers text. Marxists Internet Archive ↗

Four years earlier, in The Tasks of the Russian Social-Democrats, Lenin introduced the same line with “It was said long ago that…”. He was quoting it as an established saying, not presenting it as his own new idea. He does not say who first said it. Marxists Internet Archive ↗

items.who: “There can be no revolutionary movement without revolutionary theory”
items.why: This reversed form circulates as a paraphrase. For example, William Z. Foster used it in a 1939 article on Lenin and Stalin. It is not how Lenin’s sentence reads in either English translation. Wikiquote ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Lenin’s, from What Is To Be Done? (1902), Chapter I. The wording with “a” is the 1929 International Publishers translation. See the scan ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: What Is To Be Done? was Lenin’s pamphlet against the “Economists.” In his view, these were Russian Marxists who put day-to-day practical work ahead of theory. The sentence opens his argument that the movement needs a fully thought-out theory, and he immediately says it “cannot be insisted upon too strongly” at a time of fashionable opportunism.

The same paragraph goes on to name three reasons theory mattered especially to Russian Social-Democrats: the party was still forming, the movement was international and had to learn critically from other countries, and Russia faced tasks no other socialist party had faced. The slogan later became one of the most quoted lines in Marxist–Leninist literature.
context.pull: This cannot be insisted upon too strongly.
